Conversation guide

Sexual preferences

Practice describing what feels comfortable, asking about a partner's preferences, and accepting that your answers may differ.

Start six-round practiceRead the guide
UnderstandPracticeGet support

You can name what you want while making a different answer welcome. Agreement grows through asking and listening.

Why this topic can feel awkward · Read the guide

A common concern

“How do I say what I like without sounding critical or demanding?”

An example of a question you might have.

Use your own experience as the starting point

You can talk about preferences with simple phrases such as 'I like,' 'I would prefer,' or 'I'm curious about.' This describes your experience without assuming what a partner should enjoy. You can also share what you do not want or do not yet know. A conversation can happen outside a sexual situation, when there is less pressure to make an immediate decision.

Curiosity leaves space for no

Ask your partner what feels comfortable and listen to the answer. Sharing a preference is an invitation to communicate, not an agreement to act on it. You may have different interests, and either person can decline without needing to defend that choice. Consent remains specific and ongoing: even something someone liked before should not be treated as an automatic yes today.

Learning context: Berkeley UHS, SHEP, and PATH to Care.

About this story

Six rounds of sharing preferences, repairing misunderstandings, and making room for different needs.

You are Maya, 22, and Eli is 23. You are Berkeley students who have been dating for a few weeks. Sitting on a campus bench after studying, you want to discuss a slower pace and more verbal check-ins before your next date.
